article.Citation: Alper KR, Stajic M, Gill JR. Fatalities Temporally Associated with the Ingestion of Ibogaine. Journal of Forensic Sciences. 2012.
article.Title: Fatalities Temporally Associated with the Ingestion of Ibogaine

ae_events.Description: Fatal acute ibogaine intoxication (single-agent or with non-drug comorbid contributing factors, e.g. cardiovascular disease); death within hours of ingestion.
Fatal multidrug intoxication combining ibogaine with opioids (morphine, methadone, fentanyl), cocaine, and/or benzodiazepines (diazepam); death within hours of ingestion.
Fatal cardiac event (myocardial infarction, arrhythmia, or cardiorespiratory arrest) as proximate or contributing cause of death, often with preexisting cardiovascular disease.
Suspected fatal pulmonary thromboembolism per clinical/death-certificate diagnosis; autopsy inadequate to confirm in any of the three cases.
Witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure c. 17h post-ingestion, possibly related to alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal, in a case that was ultimately fatal.
Acute hemorrhagic pancreatitis complicating chronic alcoholism, fatal, occurring during ibogaine treatment.
Hemorrhagic complications of duodenal ulcer, possibly with increased intracranial pressure from ventricular obstruction; fatal outcome.

article.IsObservational: Retrospective case series based on systematic review of autopsy, toxicology, and investigative reports for a consecutive series of ibogaine-associated fatalities identified 1990-2008 via a treatment-provider network, OCME referral, and literature search; no randomization or research-administered intervention, so this is naturalistic real-world data (observational), not an RCT.
article.Condition: 15 of 19 decedents took ibogaine for opioid detoxification (the predominant indication; 4 of these were also alcohol-dependent, 3 cocaine-dependent, 1 methamphetamine-dependent); 2 used ibogaine for spiritual/psychological purposes with no substance-abuse history; 2 for unknown reasons but with a substance-abuse history. Coded as 'Opioid' based on the plurality/predominant indication, though the population is mixed and not exclusively opioid-focused.
article.Substance: Ibogaine administered as the HCl salt in 14 cases, Tabernanthe iboga alkaloid extract in 2 (cases #4, #14), dried root bark in 2 (cases #13, #16), and a powder of ambiguous form (extract vs. root bark) in 1 (case #6).
article.N: This is a case series comprising all 19 known fatalities temporally associated with ibogaine ingestion identified via the study's case-finding methodology; N set to 19 as every identified case is included and individually analyzed in Table 1/Results.
article.AE_denominator: Set equal to N (19) because every identified fatality has a known death outcome (the article's core 'AE'), even though toxicology/autopsy sub-data were unavailable for some (full toxicology missing in 8, autopsy missing in 5). The true population of ibogaine users at risk (denominator for incidence) is not reported/unknown -- the authors note their broader ethnographic survey may have missed 20-30% of total treatments, but do not give a total-exposed denominator.
article.ArmScope: Single-arm case series of ibogaine-exposed fatalities with no comparator group; psychedelic_arm applies by default since all values are restricted to ibogaine-exposed individuals.
article.PctFemale: 4 of 19 decedents were female (15 M, 4 F) = 21.05%, rounded to 21.1.
article.PctBIPOC: Race/ethnicity of decedents is not reported anywhere in the article.
article.NumDistinctAEs: This article is a case series where death is the outcome shared by all 19 participants. Rather than counting each of the 19 individual deaths as a separate 'AE', NumDistinctAEs=7 reflects the distinct proximate-cause/event categories the authors describe across the series: (1) acute ibogaine intoxication alone, (2) multidrug intoxication (ibogaine + other abused substances), (3) cardiac event, (4) suspected pulmonary embolism, (5) witnessed seizure, (6) hemorrhagic pancreatitis, (7) duodenal ulcer hemorrhage -- consistent with the codebook's 'distinct AE type' counting convention (cf. '12 participants reported headache is 1 type'). These categories are not mutually exclusive (a single case can have both an ibogaine-intoxication proximate cause and cardiac disease as a contributing factor), so per-category participant counts sum to more than 19.
article.NParticipantsWithAE: All 19 decedents had the qualifying AE of death (the shared/defining outcome of this case series).
article.WorstSeverity: Severe because every AE category involves death (CTCAE grade 5-equivalent) or a life-threatening/serious event, unambiguously meeting the FDA 'death' seriousness criterion.

ae_events.Alper 2012_AE01: Severe because these are deaths (meets FDA 'death' seriousness criterion). n=6 based on cases where Table 1's proximate cause of death is 'Acute ibogaine intoxication' without a co-occurring abused-drug intoxication label (cases #1, #4, #5, #6, #13, #19).
ae_events.Alper 2012_AE02: n=4 based on cases whose Table 1 proximate cause of death explicitly cites 'combined effects' of ibogaine and named co-ingestants: case #2 (morphine), #3 (opiates/cocaine), #16 (methadone/diazepam), #17 (fentanyl/diazepam).
ae_events.Alper 2012_AE03: n=6 taken directly from the article's own statement (Discussion) that 'Cardiac disease was a contributing condition or proximate cause in six deaths'; the specific six case numbers are not individually itemized by the authors beyond this aggregate count, so exact case-by-case attribution could not be independently verified.
ae_events.Alper 2012_AE04: n=3 taken directly from the article's statement that pulmonary thromboembolism 'was the reported cause of death in three deaths (cases #7, #12, and #18)'. The article explicitly notes autopsy was inadequate to confirm PE in all three (death-certificate/clinical diagnosis only) -- flagged here but still coded MeetsFDASerious=Y since death itself independently meets the seriousness criterion regardless of diagnostic certainty.
ae_events.Alper 2012_AE05: Case #10 had a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure ~17h post-ingestion, discussed at length as possibly related to alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal (n=1). The Discussion also speculates that partial seizures 'originating from the temporal lobe' may have contributed to case #14's death, but this is explicitly hedged by the authors as one of several uncertain/possible contributing factors (alongside hemorrhagic ulcer and increased intracranial pressure) rather than a confirmed seizure, so it was not added to this AE's count -- captured instead under AE07.
ae_events.Alper 2012_AE06: Case #8 only; hemorrhagic pancreatitis was both the official and proximate cause of death in a patient with chronic alcoholism, occurring during ibogaine treatment.
ae_events.Alper 2012_AE07: Case #14 only; the autopsy was 'not conclusive regarding proximal cause of death' -- hemorrhagic complications of a duodenal ulcer, increased intracranial pressure from third-ventricle obstruction (choroid plexus papilloma), and/or temporal-lobe partial seizures were all listed as possible/contributing factors. Coded as its own AE type (duodenal ulcer hemorrhage) since that was the article's leading candidate explanation; the seizure and intracranial-pressure elements of this same case are noted here rather than double-counted as separate AE rows given how entangled and speculative they are in the source text.
